sentences: As the city prepares for Christmas, newspapers report the theft of a near-priceless gemstone, the "famous jewel", from the countess's hotel suite.
The police arrest the suspect, a plumber with a criminal record who was in the Countess's room repairing a fireplace grate.

Meanwhile, at the detective's lodgings, the doctor finds the detective contemplating a battered old hat brought to him by the messenger, a commissionaire who seeks the detective's help in returning it and a Christmas goose to their rightful owners after he found them the previous night in the street after a scuffle.
A tag on the goose reading "For the hat owner's wife" is of little assistance, as the name is a very common one.

Ultimately, the messenger takes the goose home for dinner and the detective keeps the hat to study as an intellectual exercise, deducing the hat owner's age, social standing, intellect, and domestic status.
An excited messenger bursts in, having found the stolen gem in the goose's crop.

That evening when the hat owner appears in response to advertisements placed by the detective in the city newspapers, the detective returns his hat and offers him a new goose, which he happily accepts.

The hat owner's refusal to take the original bird's entrails leads the detective to believe that he knew nothing of the theft and that he has been truthful in his claim of having purchased the goose at a pub.
The detective and the doctor visit the pub, whose proprietor states that he bought the goose and several others from a dealer in a market district.
However, the dealer refuses to help, complaining that he has been repeatedly pestered by another man about geese he sold to the pub.
Realising that he is not the only one aware of the goose's importance, the detective tricks the dealer into revealing that it was supplied to him by its breeder, a poultry woman of a suburb.
The pestering man visits the stall and identifies himself to the detective as the hotel servant, head attendant at the hotel from which the gem was stolen, who had testified that he found it missing.

Upon being taken to the detective's lodgings and shown the gem, a remorseful hotel servant admits that he and his accomplice, the Countess's maid, had contrived to steal it and frame the suspect, whose criminal past would make him an easy scapegoat.
During a visit to his sister, the poultry woman, the hotel servant had concealed the gem by feeding it to a goose she had promised him as a gift, but confused the bird with another.
By the time he realised his mistake, his goose had already been sold.
As it is Christmas, the detective takes pity on the hotel servant and allows him to flee the country, concluding that the man is too frightened by what happened to offend again.
The detective is confident that the case against the suspect will be dismissed for lack of evidence once the hotel servant fails to appear in court as a prosecution witness.
In April 1883, the detective and the doctor rise early one morning to meet a young woman named the client, who is in great fear of her life.
She explains that her mother married her stepfather, the physician, in the colony when the client and her twin sister the twin were two years old.
The physician is the impoverished sole survivor of a formerly wealthy but ill-tempered, violent, and amoral aristocratic Anglo-Saxon family in a southern county.
He had served time in an Indian prison for killing his Indian butler in a rage.
Afterwards, the physician had moved to the home country and retired after the client's mother was killed in a railway accident eight years prior.
The sisters lived at the heavily mortgaged and debt ridden physician's family estate of the manor; the physician's violent temper and physical strength make him a terror in the local village.
The sisters did not live happily, but when the twin got engaged two years prior, things promised to improve.
Shortly before her wedding day, the twin confided in the client that she had heard a low whistle in the night.
That same night, the client was startled out of bed by her sister's scream.
The client found the twin at her door, warning of "the speckled band" shortly before dying.
The official inquest was unable to determine the cause of death: the room was securely locked both inside and outside, and the doctors could find no poison.
Two years later, it was the client's turn to get engaged.
However, when the physician started repairs outside the house, she had to move into the twin's old room.
One night, she heard the whistle that heralded her sister's death; terrified, she approached the detective the next day.
After the detective agrees to take the case, he is visited by the physician, who threatens to harm him if he interferes.
Undaunted, the detective leaves for the courthouse to examine the client's mother's will; because of the fall in investment prices the yearly income of £1,100, is not more than £750.
Each daughter can claim an income of £250, in case of marriage, and the physician would not have much to live on.
He and the doctor then travel to the manor, where he scrutinizes the premises.
Within the client's room, he discovers her bed is anchored to the floor, an unconnected bell cord has been installed, and a ventilator hole connects her room to the physician's.
In the physician's room, they notice a large safe and a saucer of milk.
While discussing his findings with the doctor, the detective remarks that the physician is comparable to Drs.
A notorious poisoner and another notorious poisoner.
The detective instructs the client to stay in the twin's old room until the physician has retired for the night, then to show a light at the window and return to her room.
Once she has done so, the detective and the doctor sneak onto the grounds and climb into the twin's room.
After a tense wait, they hear a slight metallic noise and see a dim light through the ventilator, followed by a hissing sound.
The detective lights a candle and strikes at the bell cord, and they hear a terrifying scream.

The detective and the doctor go to the physician's room, where they see the "speckled band" – a fictional venomous swamp adder which the detective identifies as the most poisonous snake in the colony.
Angered by the detective's blows, the snake had attacked the physician, killing him.

In order to prevent his daughters from marrying and so reducing his annual income, he had trained the snake to crawl through the ventilator and down the bell cord, bite anyone sleeping in the twin's bed, and return at his whistle (using the milk as a lure).
He kept it in the safe during the day as a safety precaution.
The official inquest rules the physician met his fate while indiscreetly playing with a dangerous pet.

Though the detective also admits to indirectly killing the physician, he does not foresee it troubling him and chooses not to tell the police the physician's full motive to spare the client any further grief.

In the summer of 1889, a young city man and consultant hydraulic engineer, the engineer, is brought to the doctor's home one morning to receive medical attention for a severed thumb he sustained the previous night.
Once the doctor has tended to the wound, he takes the engineer to see the detective so the latter can hear the details of the night's events.

The engineer was visited by a man who identified himself as the colonel and offered to pay him 50 guineas (£, ) to examine a hydraulic press at a country house in a village, in a nearby county that the colonel claimed was used to compress fuller's earth into bricks.
Despite his misgivings and doubts about the machine's true purpose, the engineer felt compelled to accept the offer, as his business was newly established and he had little work.
Upon arriving at an appointed train station, the engineer was picked up by the colonel in a carriage with frosted glass windows.
They traveled what seemed to be a considerable distance, estimated by the engineer to be 12 miles.
After they arrived at the house, a woman warned the engineer to leave, but he disregarded her.
The colonel and a man introduced as the secretary took the engineer to the hydraulic press.
The engineer made recommendations on how to fix it, but did not believe it was being used to compress fuller's earth, as the engine was far too powerful for such a purpose.
Closer examination confirmed that the device was used to process metal.
He confronted the colonel, who then tried to kill him with the press.
After the woman helped the engineer escape, making a reference to a "last time", a murderous colonel pursued him with a cleaver.
The engineer climbed out a second-storey window and hung on to the sill, preparing to drop to the ground, but instead fell when the colonel severed his thumb.
Surviving the fall, the engineer passed out while fleeing among the rosebushes and later awoke by a hedge near the train station.
Once the engineer finishes his story, the detective deduces that the colonel and his allies are counterfeiters, and their machine was used to mint false coins.
The police confirm that a gang has been producing half crowns in large amounts, but could not be tracked until now.

From the engineer's account of the colonel's carriage horse being fresh and well-groomed, the detective concludes that the criminals are located near the station, and that the 12-mile drive with frosted glass windows was intended to disguise their location.
Checking the newspapers helps identify the "last time" the woman spoke about; a hydraulic engineer left his lodgings a year prior, and has never been seen since.
The detective, the doctor, and the police travel to the house the engineer described, only to find it ablaze due to the engineer's oil lamp being crushed by the press.
Their operation ruined, the counterfeiters fled in the direction of a large town, in the nearby county, taking several large boxes that the detective believes may have held their coins.
The engineer laments the loss of both his thumb and the 50 guineas, but the detective reassures him that he has gained a compelling story that he can tell for the rest of his life.
The nobleman comes to the detective and the doctor for help after his bride, the heiress, disappeared during their wedding reception.
He explains that the dollar princess—heiress to a large western-state mining fortune—traveled to his country, eager to marry him after they met in a western city.
However, the heiress became uncharacteristically sharp with the nobleman following the wedding, during which she had dropped her bouquet and a gentleman in the front row returned it to her.
During the post-wedding breakfast at the nobleman's father-in-law's home, the heiress spoke with her maid before claiming "a sudden indisposition" and retired to her room.
Not long after, she is discovered to have disappeared.
Additionally, her wedding dress and ring were found washed ashore at a park lake, leading the inspector of the police headquarters to drag the river for the heiress's body.
Despite the inspector and the doctor's confusion, the detective easily deduces what happened, having dealt with similar cases before.
Upon locating the heiress, he forces her to reveal to the nobleman that the mystery man, the miner.
The miner, was her previous husband.
Years prior, following their own wedding, the miner had left to become a prospector.

After he was reported killed following an Apache raid on the mining camp he worked at, the heiress assumed it was true and eventually met the nobleman even though she was still in love with the miner.
Meanwhile, the miner was captured by the Apache, but escaped and followed the heiress to the capital to reunite with her.
She recognised him instantly, though he gestured her to stay silent to avoid causing a scandal and secretly passed a note to her while returning her bouquet.
She subsequently faked her death to be with the miner again.
The detective convinces the heiress to be more honest and apologize to the nobleman.
However, he refuses to accept, feeling that he had been ill used.

A banker named the financier makes a loan of £50,000 to a client from one of the "highest, noblest, most exalted names in the country," implied to be a member of the British royal family and, thus, a son of the queen and an heir to the throne.
The client leaves the beryl coronet, described as one of the "most precious public possessions of the empire," as collateral.
Feeling his bank's personal safe is insufficient to protect such a rare and valuable piece of jewellery, he takes it to his home in a suburb and keeps it in his dressing room.
However, he and his niece the young woman later find his son the young man holding the coronet, seemingly trying to bend it, with three beryls missing from it.
A panicked financier seeks out the detective for help.
Despite the damning evidence against the young man, who refuses to give a statement, the detective is unconvinced.

With the threat of the financier's reputation being besmirched and a national scandal weighing heavily on his mind, the detective determines the young man could not have broken the coronet on his own without making noise, notices footprints in the snow outside the financier's home, and considers the financier's servants, the young woman, and the young man's rakish friend the aristocrat as potential suspects.
Eventually, the detective concludes the aristocrat is a notorious criminal who conspired with the young woman, unaware of his real identity, to steal the coronet.
The young man caught the pair in the act and broke the coronet while trying to take it back from the aristocrat before taking the blame for the young woman out of love for her.
Though the aristocrat and the young woman escape justice, the detective is convinced they will receive their punishment in due time.

He later buys back the missing beryls from a fence that the aristocrat sold them to, receives compensation from the financier, and tells him to apologize to the young man for assuming he was the thief.

The governess visits the detective for advice on whether she should accept a unique governess job with a substantial initial salary of £100 a year, on the condition that she cut her hair short, among other strange provisos.
When she initially refuses, the man who made the offer, the employer, increases the offer to £120.
Despite her suspicions, the governess ultimately agrees, and leaves for a southern county to work at the employer's countryside estate, the manor.
The detective advises her to contact him via telegram, should she need him.
After a fortnight, the detective receives a message from the governess, beseeching him to see her in a nearby city.
After they reunite, she explains that the employer would sometimes make her wear an electric blue dress and sit in the front room, with her back to the front window.
Suspecting she was not supposed to see something outside, she used a small mirror shard hidden in her handkerchief to confirm and witnessed a man standing by the nearby road looking at the house.

Additionally, the employer's wife never seemed to smile, the governess's six-year-old charge was astonishingly cruel to small animals, and the governess found a cut-off tress of hair similar to her own in a locked drawer.
Furthermore, the dog, a deliberately-starved and vicious Mastiff that only the drunken manservant the keeper could control, was let loose every night to prowl the grounds.
As such, the governess was ordered not to cross the threshold after dark.
The governess had also been uneasy about a forbidden wing of the house where the windows were either dirty or shuttered.
At one point, the employer emerged from it, looking perturbed, and claimed he was using it as a darkroom.
Unconvinced, the governess entered the wing when the keeper left his keys in the door, only to be frightened into fleeing by a moving shadow on the other side of a locked door.
She collided with the employer, who attempted to comfort her and ascertain what she might have found out.
His overacting aroused the governess's suspicions, confirmed when he suddenly threatened to feed her to the dog if she entered the wing again.
Accepting the case, the detective deduces someone is being held prisoner in the mystery wing.

He further deduces the employer hired the governess to impersonate his daughter the prisoner, whom the governess was unaware of and strongly resembled, to convince the stranger outside that the prisoner is not interested in seeing him.
Joined by the governess and the doctor, the detective breaks into the mystery wing, but it is empty.
The employer enters; deducing the prisoner has escaped and believing the trio helped her, he tries to sic the dog on them.
However, the dog had been starved for longer than usual and attacks its master, until the doctor kills it with his revolver.
Later, the keeper's wife confirms the detective's theory, and reveals when the prisoner came of age, she was to receive an annuity from her late mother's will.
The employer tried to force her to sign control of the inheritance over to him, resulting in the prisoner falling ill with brain fever and having her hair cut off.
He subsequently tried to keep her away from her fiancé the suitor and hired the governess to maintain appearances.
It was the keeper's wife who helped the prisoner escape and flee with her fiancé.

Afterward, the prisoner marries her fiancé; the employer survives as an invalid being cared for by his second wife; and the governess becomes the principal of an all-girls' school in a provincial town, which meets with "considerable success".

The detective and his partner, the doctor, travel by train to the moorland district to investigate a crime of disappearance of the great race horse the champion and the murder of the horse's trainer, the trainer.
The detective and the doctor arrive at the stables, from where the champion is missing.
The bookmaker had come to the moorland district (and specifically to the stables) to gather information about the champion and his stablemate the other horse.
He had approached both the trainer's maid and a stable boy the night of the horse's disappearance and has been arrested for the murder.
To the detective, there seem to be a number of facts that do not fit the case against the bookmaker, damning as it looks.
It seems odd that he would lead the horse out on to the moor simply to injure or kill him, which could be done in his stall.
Had he stolen the animal, what good would such a famous thoroughbred be to him?
Why has an exhaustive search of the neighbourhood not turned up the champion?
What has the bookmaker done with him?
The detective soon tracks down the champion; his tracks (along with a man's) are clearly visible in the soil, albeit intermittently.
The detective also deduces why the police could not find the horse, despite having looked right at him.
The detective ensures the champion's safety, and turns his mind to other aspects of the case.
The trainer, the champion's late trainer, has been killed by a blow to the skull, assumed to have been administered by the bookmaker with his "heavy cane", a club-like walking stick.
The bookmaker's cravat is also found in the trainer's hand, and the latter's coat is found draped over a furze bush.
A knife is found at the crime scene—a peculiarly delicate-looking one, with a small blade.
The doctor, from his medical experience, identifies it as a cataract knife used for the most delicate surgery—useful as it is for that purpose, it would be unsuitable as a weapon.
The trainer also seems to have gashed himself in the hip with it.
One of the stable lads, the stable lad, was on guard duty the night of the crime, but he proves to have been drugged with powdered opium placed in his supper.
No one else who ate the curried mutton made at the trainer's house that evening suffered any ill effects, but the stable lad was in a profound stupor well into the next day.
The trainer's pockets contained a tallow candle and a milliner's bill for (among other things) a 22-guinea dress, made out to one customer.
There is the curious incident with the dog, and a problem with the sheep kept at the stable: The boy who looks after them tells the detective that three of his animals have become suddenly lame.
The detective's powers unravel the mystery and lay bare what villainies there are to be exposed.
He visits the milliners' shop in the capital and determines, using the trainer's photograph, that the trainer posed as the customer.
This establishes his motive: He had a mistress with expensive tastes and tried to rig the race to earn himself a large sum of money.

The curried mutton was a clue; only such a spicy dish could have masked the taste of powdered opium and it was impossible for the bookmaker to arrange a highly seasoned meal that evening for his purposes.
Therefore, someone in the household must have conceived the idea, namely the trainer.
The "curious incident of the dog in the night-time" is easily explained: the dog made no noise because no stranger was there.
The detective explains, "I had grasped the significance of the silence of the dog, for one true inference invariably suggests others ...
Obviously, the midnight visitor was someone whom the dog knew well".
It was the trainer who removed the champion from his stall and led him out onto the moor.

The trainer's purpose in doing this was to use the cataract knife to inflict a slight injury upon one of the horse's legs, rendering him temporarily lame in a way that would be undetectable on examination and thus likely put down to strain.
He had thought to use the bookmaker's cravat (which the latter dropped when he was expelled from the stables) as a sling to hold the horse's leg to cut it.
The trainer was killed when the horse, sensing that something was wrong, panicked and kicked the trainer in the head.
The lame sheep had been used by the trainer for practice.
The owner's main concern, of course, is getting his horse back.
The detective chooses not to tell the owner where his horse has been (although he has known all along) until after the big race, which is won by the champion.
At first, the Colonel does not recognise his horse, since the animal's distinguishing white markings have been covered with dye.
The horse had been looked after by one of the Colonel's neighbours, the neighbour, who had found him wandering the moor and hidden him in his barn.
The detective then explains the details of the case step-by-step to the satisfaction of the Colonel, the doctor and the inspector.
The inspector is one of the more competent police detectives with whom the detective works in the course of his career.
The landlady of the town receives a parcel in the post that contains two severed human ears packed in coarse salt.
The inspector of the police force suspects a prank by three medical students whom the landlady was forced to evict because of their unruly behaviour.
The parcel was sent from the port city, the city of origin of one of the former boarders.
Upon examining the parcel himself, the detective is convinced that it is evidence of a serious crime.

He reasons that a medical student with access to a dissection laboratory would likely use something other than plain salt to preserve human remains, and would be able to make a more precise cut than the roughly hacked ears suggest.
The address on the package, roughly written and with a spelling correction, suggests to the detective that the sender lacks education and is unfamiliar with the town.
He further deduces that this person is a sailor, based on the particular method of tarring and knotting the string.

A few questions to the landlady, a few observations, a cable to another city, and an attempt to visit the landlady's sister the second sister (thwarted by the latter's sudden illness) convince the detective that the ears belong to the landlady's other sister, the married sister, and her extramarital lover, and that they have been murdered.
He concludes that the married sister's estranged husband, the husband, is the murderer, and that the husband had sent the ears to the sisters' house in the town (addressing it merely to "the initial.
the surname"), not knowing that the second sister had moved away.

The husband, who is an unpleasant man when drunk, had meant to horrify the second sister because he ultimately blamed her for causing the trouble that led him to kill the married sister and her lover.
After receiving an answer to his cable, the detective gives the inspector a note and asks him not to mention the detective's name in connection with the case due to its simplicity.
Two days later, he receives an envelope from the inspector, which contains a note stating that the husband has been arrested and a copy of his confession.
The husband is indeed a sailor, and the port city was the first port where he had the chance to post the parcel.
The inspector, acting on the detective's information, arrested him when his ship reached the capital.
According to his confession, he and the second sister began to hate each other after he rejected her advances toward him.
The second sister then began to plant suspicions in the married sister's mind concerning the husband's fidelity and introduced her to another sailor, the lover.

Despite the husband's orders that the lover stay away from the household, he and the married sister went out rowing one day; the husband followed them onto the water, killed them both, and sent an ear from each corpse to the second sister's old address in the town.
As the detective finishes reading the husband's confession, he muses to the doctor, "What object is served by this circle of misery and violence and fear?"
He has no immediate answer, wondering if human reason will ever be able to find one.
The detective, bored due to a want of cases, returns home from a walk with the doctor early in spring to find he has missed a visitor but that the caller has left his pipe behind.

From it, the detective deduces that he was disturbed of mind (because he forgot the pipe); that he valued it highly (because he had repaired it with silver bands which cost more than the pipe cost, rather than replacing it, when it was broken); that he was muscular, left-handed, had excellent teeth, was careless in his habits (because of the tooth marks in the pipe stem and the burn patterns on the pipe bowl) and did not need to practice economy (because the pipe is packed with an expensive blend of tobacco).
None of these deductions are particularly germane to the story: they are merely the detective's logical exercises.
When the visitor, the client (whose name the detective observed from his hatband) returns, the detective and the doctor hear the story of the client's deception by his wife the wife.
She had been previously married in the far country, but her husband and child had died of yellow fever, whereupon she returned to the home country and met and married the client.
Their marriage had been blissful until the wife asked for £100 and begged him not to ask why.
Two months later, the wife was caught conducting secret liaisons with the occupants of a cottage near the client's house in the village.
The client has seen a mysterious yellow-faced person in this cottage.
Overcome with jealousy, he breaks in and finds the place empty.
However, the room where he saw the mysterious figure is very comfortable and well furnished, with a portrait of his wife on the mantelpiece.
The detective, after sending the client home with instructions to wire for him if the cottage was reoccupied, confides in the doctor his belief that the mysterious figure is the wife's first husband.
He postulates that the husband, having been left in the far country, has come to the home country to blackmail her.
After the client summons the detective and the doctor, the three enter the cottage, brushing aside the entreaties of the wife.
They find the strange yellow-faced character, and the detective peels the face away, showing it to be a mask, and revealing a young girl who is half-black.
It is then revealed that the wife's first husband was the late husband, an African-American lawyer, who did die in the far country, but their daughter, the girl, survived.
At the time the wife came to the home country, she could not bring the girl with her, as the child was still ill enough that the transition might have exacerbated her state.
But later, after she and the client were married, the wife got word that the girl was alive and well.

Upon hearing of this, the wife became overcome with desire to see her child again, so she asked for the hundred pounds and used it to bring the girl and her nurse to the home country, and installed them in the cottage near the client's house.

She feared, however, that the client might stop loving her if he found out that she was the mother of a mixed race child, so all the while, she had made every endeavour to keep the girl's existence a secret.
Both the doctor and the detective are touched by the client's response.
The doctor observes: ...when [the client's] answer came it was one of which I love to think.
He lifted the little child, kissed her, and then, still carrying her, he held his other hand out to his wife and turned towards the door.
"We can talk about it more comfortably at home," said he.
"I am not a very good man, wife, but I think I am a better one than you have given me credit for being."

The detective excuses himself and the doctor, and, that evening, after they have returned to their lodgings, says: Doctor, if it should ever strike you that I am getting a little overconfident in my powers, or giving less pains to a case than it deserves, kindly whisper 'the village' in my ear, and I shall be infinitely obliged to you.
A young clerk, the clerk, consults the detective with his suspicions concerning a company that has offered him a very well-paid job.

The detective, the doctor and the clerk travel by train to the provincial city, where the job has so far been based, and the clerk explains that the capital-city brokerage firm at which he worked had gone out of business, leaving him unemployed.
He eventually secured a new post with another such firm in the financial district, the brokerage, without an interview.

Before taking up the job, he was approached by the recruiter, who offered him a better-paid managership with a newly established hardware distribution company, to be based in a neighbouring country, with a £100 advance on salary.
At the recruiter's request, the clerk wrote a document accepting the position and also agreed not to send a letter of resignation to the brokerage.
The clerk was sent to the provincial city to meet the recruiter's brother the employer, a company co-founder.
He immediately commenced his duties, but was concerned about the unprofessional aspects of the business and its sparse offices.
Having noticed that both brothers had a gold-filled tooth at the same position in their mouths, he suspected that they might be the same man.

As the trio arrive at the office in the provincial city, with the detective and the doctor presented as fellow job-seekers, the employer goes into shock after buying and reading the evening newspaper.
He withdraws and attempts to hang himself, but the doctor is able to revive him.

The detective concludes that the story of the brothers is a fabrication and that there is only one "man of that name," who has posed as both of them in the hope that the clerk might dismiss the similarities between them as a family resemblance.

The detective further deduces that the whole point of the exercise has been to get the clerk out of the capital and obtain a sample of his handwriting so that an imposter can gain employment at the brokerage (hence the request for the clerk to not officially resign his post).
The imposter is to break into the company safe and steal the large stockpile of valuable securities kept within.
From the newspaper, they learn that the brokerage has suffered an attempted robbery, culminating in the murder of the weekend watchman and the capture of the thief.
Having recently completed a prison sentence, a forger/safecracker named the thief and his brother concocted the scheme to steal the securities.

The thief took the job intended for the clerk so he could gain the information needed to carry out the heist, while his brother posed as both the recruiter and the employer to keep the clerk occupied.
Bonds worth nearly £100,000 were taken, together with large amounts of scrip in mines and other companies, but the police recovered them from the thief.
Sending the clerk out to notify the police so they can come to arrest the thief's brother, the detective comments, "Human nature is a strange mixture, doctor.
You see that even a villain and murderer can inspire such affection that his brother turns to suicide when he learns that his neck is forfeited."
